label: FY2027 Q1 (27 Jun–25 Sep 2026)
asOf: close of $51.47 on 2 Nov 2026, $59.12 after hours (Investing.com)
headline: Revenue tripled and orders keep rising, yet the stock halved before the report: on burn-in for AI chips, the market only half believes

points.b: The hotter AI chips run, the more they need burn-in
points.t: Burn-in stresses chips at high heat and voltage to weed out early failures before shipping; an AI processor draws over a kilowatt and costs tens of thousands of dollars, so each failure costs more.

Package-level Sonoma systems are installed at more than a dozen a month for one hyperscaler; the lead AI customer for wafer-level FOX-XP keeps expanding, and another large AI chip maker will evaluate it in volume production.
It closed at $99.62 at the end of September and $51.47 on report day, down 48%, with no guidance cut in between. It rebounded about 15% after hours.

reaction: Stock: closed at $51.47 (−6.2%) on report day and rose to $59.12 (+14.9%) after hours. Revenue was 23% above consensus, EPS nearly 3x, and full-year guidance moved to the top of the range. In the month before the report the stock fell about half from $99.62 on 30 Sep, with no negative company news; it had already gone from about $20 to about $100 in the first three quarters of 2026, so swings this large are normal for it. Next day (3 Nov) it closed at $65.11, +26.5%, against +2.0% for the semiconductor ETF (SMH). Consensus from Investing.com: EPS $0.10, revenue $26.82M.

segments.title: Revenue mix
segments.take: Systems and consumables each added about half of the increase. Consumables rose from 24% to 41% of revenue: the more systems installed, the more WaferPaks and burn-in boards customers buy each year, and that revenue is steadier.

rows.why: FOX-XP wafer-level systems, automated aligners and package-level Sonoma systems. Management said customers asked to pull some shipments into Q1.
WaferPak full-wafer contactors, DiePaks, burn-in modules and boards. Expected at about 35% for the year, up to 50% in a strong year; the long-term model is about 30%.

segments.note: The company doesn't split revenue by AI, silicon photonics, SiC or GaN. Year-ago systems and consumables are backed out from the 24% consumables share management gave. FY26 silicon carbide revenue was under 10% of revenue (about $5M).

extras.title: Where it sits in the AI loop
extras.take: Aehr does the last step in the chip layer: burn-in testing before chips ship. Its customers are hyperscalers building their own AI chips and AI processor makers, so it rides the ramp of in-house chips like TPU, Trainium and MTIA, not just NVIDIA.

items.b: A winner from in-house AI chips
items.w: The lead Sonoma customer is a hyperscaler ramping its first in-house AI processor; the second has qualified and will be bigger. In the late-October reporting season, Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium, Microsoft's Maia and Meta's own chips were all ramping (see the NVIDIA and cloud pages).

items.b: More power, more need for burn-in
items.w: Sonoma handles up to 2,000 watts per device. The bigger, pricier and hotter a chip, the more a failure in the data center costs, and the more customers want to “bake” it before it ships.

items.b: Moving onto the test giants' turf
items.w: The mainstream AI chip test platforms are Advantest's V93000 and Teradyne's UltraFLEX, with system-level test (SLT) as another option. Aehr's pitch is burn-in at the wafer stage, weeding out bad die before packaging.

The first AI wafer-level systems sit at a leading global test house, and the new evaluation customer will also install at a Taiwan test house. Aehr has leased new space and added service staff in Taiwan. Its risk statements name geopolitical conditions affecting Taiwan and Southeast Asia.

items.b: Silicon photonics is the second line
items.w: Photonics chips also need wafer-level burn-in; several customers added FOX-XP orders this quarter, including a global networking leader. It is the same demand as the optical module ramp on the Fabrinet page.

extras.title: Where growth comes from
extras.take: Backlog already covers most of FY27's $150M; the stock is betting on the next big customer: if the AI accelerator maker evaluating in Taiwan goes into production, its orders could exceed all current customers combined. It is close to a yes-or-no outcome.

items.w: Effective backlog was $109.3M as of 1 November; about $117M of revenue is still needed for the year, mostly covered. Capacity supports more than $150M, and a Southeast Asian contract maker can add over 20 Sonoma systems a month.
Up from 37.5% a year ago on more consumables and scale. Q2 will be lower than Q1 because of a heavy Sonoma mix; about 48.5% for the year.

Management's illustration: every 1 million chips a year needs about 5–10 systems, worth $35–70M in systems and consumables; 2027 AI accelerators run about 25 million units and CPUs about double. That's the company's framing, not an order.
FY27 revenue $150M with non-GAAP net income at least 20% of revenue; no multi-year targets. Management says more than a dozen customers could now place large orders, versus a handful before.

Watch whether the Taiwan evaluation slips or loses; the ramp pace of the hyperscaler's second chip; big swings in single-customer orders between quarters; and whether operating cash flow turns positive (−$3.1M this quarter on early component buying).

valuation.take: Very expensive on past profits: 24 times trailing revenue and over 170 times non-GAAP earnings, and about 58 times even on FY27 guidance. The price rests on the next big customer: if the Taiwan evaluation becomes a production order, profits could multiply again; if it doesn't, the valuation has no cushion.

scenarios.note: Bear: the Taiwan evaluation fails and the lead customer slows purchases, so revenue falls about a quarter; base: current AI customers keep expanding and photonics ramps, about 47% growth; bull: the Taiwan evaluation customer goes into production. 34.5M shares (with dilution). These assumptions are ours and are not forecasts.

pricezone.sub: FY28 EPS × our P/E; price at the 2 Nov close (before the report)
pricezone.why: The price is close to the base case: buying now, the base case gains only about 9% while the bear case loses about 75%, far more risk than reward. Near the $32.5 midpoint the base case gains about 72% and the bear case loses about 60%, a reward/risk of about 1.2; about 2.6 at the $25 low end. The outcome here is close to yes-or-no, with bear and bull nearly 9x apart, so the zone is wider than for other companies (60% from bottom to top) and further from the bear-case price. The stock has swung between $7 and $100 over the past year and a half, so multiples are a weak guide.

history.title: Against its own past 5 years
history.sub: Price/sales (TTM revenue, diluted shares), quarter ends
history.note: About 24x now, above 16 of the past 20 quarter ends, against a median of about 10x; it reached 59x at the end of June. Aehr's fiscal quarters end in February, May, August and November, about a month off calendar quarter ends. We calculate it from SEC revenue, diluted shares and quarter-end closes.

cash.title: Bookings and backlog
cash.note: Operating cash flow was −$3.05M: receivables rose $10.7M and inventory $9.0M as the company bought long-lead parts early. It paid $4.47M of employee tax withholding on vested shares. Cash was only about $25M a year ago; most of today's $105M came from an equity raise over the past year.

changes.now: Bought a full test cell to install at a Taiwan test house in early 2027, “one of the largest burn-in opportunities Aehr has ever pursued”.

changes.before: Only a handful of customers could place large orders.
changes.now: More than a dozen across AI processors, silicon photonics, SiC and GaN.

changes.before: Flash wafer-level burn-in evaluation went well; proposed a high-bandwidth flash solution.
changes.now: Flash is slower than expected (customer capacity and delayed high-bandwidth flash volumes); a new wafer-level burn-in opportunity in HBM base dies.
